newsitem.title: INDIA: Strong rupee has hurt India competitiveness-I-Sec.
newsitem.headline: Strong rupee has hurt India competitiveness-I-Sec.

text.p: A strong rupee has hurt India's export competitiveness, securities firm ICICI Securities and Finance Company (I-Sec), an affiliate of investment bank J.P. Morgan, said on Tuesday.

"With the rupee at somewhat the same levels now as it was in January 1996 and an average inflation rate of roughtly six percent over this period (implying higher input costs) India's export competitiveness in international markets has certainly been affected," I-Sec said in a debt market update.
The exchange rate has been fairly stable between 35.50-35.90 rupees to a dollar levels since July 1996.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI)'s recent intervention showed that the rupee's depreciation would be limited, I-Sec said.
The RBI has been buying dollars in recent months to arrest the rupee's appreciation against the dollar.
"On the contrary, the RBI would like to see the rupee depreciate gradually over the next three to six months."
It said RBI bought an estimated $600 to $800 million since the announcement of the budget on February 28.
"With an intention to keep the dollar well bid over the next six months, the RBI has been buying forward dollars all the way upto September maturity..," I-Sec said in its report.
"As far as foreign exchange management is concerned, the RBI seems to be caught between the devil and the deep sea," it said.

While RBI had to buy dollars to keep the rupee from appreciating in nominal terms (and more so in real terms), the expansionary impact on rupee liquidity and therefore on inflation needs to be neutralised, I-Sec said.
One alternative would be to liberalise imports of consumer goods, which would absorb dollar funds and will also restrain inflation.
Analysts say India is likely to lift quantitative restrictions on the import of consumer goods in its export import policy for 1997/98 (April-March) to be announced next month.
"Another slightly difficult decision for the RBI would be to discourage foreign currency deposits by re-imposing reserve requirements on these," the I-Sec report said.
